steps.say: Donor surgery favours the left kidney. Keyhole removal prefers the left side because its vein is much longer than the short right vein joining the great vein directly. Extra vein length simplifies the recipient join and improves safety, so the right kidney stays with the donor unless anatomy says otherwise.
steps.tx: Laparoscopic **donor nephrectomy** (keyhole living-donor removal) preferentially harvests the left kidney for its significantly **longer left renal vein** (extra venous length) versus the short right vein draining directly into the IVC. Extra length simplifies the recipient join and improves safety, so the right kidney stays unless anatomy says otherwise.

rows: Right taken only if anatomy dictates

steps.say: The new kidney rests in the pelvis, not the loin. It is set into the groin pocket outside the belly lining, joining its artery to the groin arteries and its vein to the groin vein. The native kidneys stay untouched, and the outside pocket keeps any leak away from the tummy.
steps.tx: **Heterotopic placement** (pelvic implantation) sets the allograft into the recipient **iliac fossa** (groin pocket) extraperitoneally, joining allograft renal artery to **external iliac anastomosis** (external or internal iliac artery join) and vein to external iliac vein. Native kidneys stay untouched, and the extraperitoneal pocket confines leaks away from the abdomen.

vis.alt: Diagram of native kidney shrinkage with pelvic renal graft and arm fistula.
vis.caption: Pelvic allograft in the iliac fossa outside the peritoneum. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: The ureter is joined to the bladder from outside. Tunnelling the donor ureter into the bladder wall with a plastic stent left across the join carries the lowest leak and blockage rates. The anti reflux tunnel plus temporary stenting protects the join while it heals.
steps.tx: Extravesical **Lich-Gregoir allograft reimplantation** (outside-bladder tunnel technique) with a **double-J stent** (temporary internal stent) across the join is the standard allograft ureter implantation, with the lowest leak and obstruction rates. The anti-reflux tunnel plus temporary stenting protects the anastomosis during healing.

vis.alt: Antegrade dye study showing nephrostomy tube and ureteral stent.
vis.caption: Stented ureter of the type protected after Lich-Gregoir implantation. Credit: Jmarchn, CC BY-SA, Wikimedia Commons.

steps.say: Narrowing comes from blood loss at harvest. Narrowing in two to five in a hundred grafts follows when stripping the donor ureter starves its lower end. The golden rule is keeping the tissue blanket around the donor ureter, because the ureter lives on that outer blood supply.
steps.tx: **Transplant ureteral stenosis** (allograft ureter narrowing) in **2% to 5%** (two to five in a hundred) follows devascularization starving distal ureter, a **ureteral ischemia** (blood-supply loss) injury from harvesting. Preserving the periureteral tissue blanket around the donor ureter is the golden rule, since the ureter lives on adventitial supply.

steps.say: Leaks are spotted with kidney numbers. Leaks in one to four in a hundred show rising blood kidney markers, groin pain, and wound wetness, and sucked out fluid shows kidney marker far above blood levels. The comparison alone tells leak from lymph swelling apart.
steps.tx: **Transplant urine leak** (anastomosis leak) in **1% to 4%** (one to four in a hundred) presents with rising creatinine, pelvic pain, and wound drainage; **drain fluid creatinine** (fluid kidney-marker test) far exceeds serum levels. Lymph mirrors blood creatinine while urine concentrates it manifold, so the number alone tells leak from lymph swelling apart.

rows: Rising creatinine, pelvic pain, wound drainage
Drain fluid creatinine far above serum
Leak from lymphocele by the number

steps.say: Lymph swellings come from unsealed channels. Swellings in one to fifteen in a hundred follow unclipped groin lymph vessels cut during exposure, and painful presses on graft vein or ureter need keyhole windowing into the tummy lining. Careful clipping at exposure prevents most of them.
steps.tx: **Lymphocele** (lymph swelling) in **1% to 15%** (one to fifteen in a hundred) follows unligated recipient iliac lymphatics; symptomatic compression of allograft vein or ureter needs laparoscopic **peritoneal fenestration** (**marsupialization**, windowing into peritoneum) for internal drainage. Meticulous lymphatic clipping at exposure prevents most cases.

rows: Fenestrate into peritoneum by keyhole surgery

steps.say: Artery narrowing mimics rejection. Graft artery narrowing shows treatment resistant high pressure and unexplained graft failure, and first treatment is balloon widening with a stent rather than open redo. The picture overlaps rejection and blockage, so fast flow on ultrasound plus a suspicious scan earns dye imaging.
steps.tx: **Transplant renal artery stenosis** (graft artery narrowing) presents with refractory hypertension and unexplained graft dysfunction; first-line care is percutaneous transluminal **angioplasty and stenting** (balloon widening with stent) over open revision. The picture overlaps rejection and obstruction, so Doppler velocity rise plus suggestive renography earns angiography.

steps.say: Vein clots kill grafts in hours. Graft vein clotting causes sudden urine stop, severe graft swelling with pain, and graft loss, striking under one to two in a hundred within two to three days. Kinks, low pressure, and thick blood are the triggers, and rescue needs instant reopening before the cortex dies.
steps.tx: **Renal vein thrombosis** (graft vein clot) causes sudden **oliguria** (urine stoppage), severe **graft swelling** (painful swollen allograft), and graft loss, striking under **1% to 2%** (one to two in a hundred) within **48 to 72 hours** (forty eight to seventy two). Kinks, hypotension, and hypercoagulability trigger it, and salvage needs immediate re-exploration with thrombectomy before cortical necrosis completes.

rows: Sudden oliguria with painful graft swelling
First 48 to 72 hours, under 1 to 2 percent
